title: Kali Springs From Her Brow
hookLine: a general undone by one syllable, and Kali springing from the goddess's own frowning brow
carry: kali is the mother's own fierce face
tomorrow: a demon whose every drop of blood becomes another demon. how do you stop him?

lines: DRAG HER HERE BY THE HAIR.
cards: One syllable: hum. That's all it takes in the sixth chapter. Furious at her vow, Shumbha sends a general named Dhumralochana with an army and an order: drag her here by the hair.
The general shouts at her to come quietly. She answers, in paraphrase: you're strong, and you've brought an army. If you take me by force, what can I do?
He rushes at her. She makes one sound, hum, and he's burned to ash. Her lion takes care of the army.
And the goddess is about to show a face the story hasn't shown yet.

teach.h: HER FACE GOES DARK AS INK.
teach.b: In the seventh chapter Shumbha sends Chanda and Munda, the servants who first told him of her, with a bigger army. They find her seated on her lion on a golden peak, smiling, and come at her with bows and swords.
Her face goes dark with anger, dark as ink. And from her frowning forehead another goddess springs out. The text describes her plainly.
Kali. Dark, gaping mouth, lolling tongue. Thin, wrapped in a tiger skin, a garland of human heads, a skull-topped staff and a sword in her hands.
Her roar fills the sky. She tears into the army, swallowing elephants whole with their riders and bells, crunching chariots in her teeth.

She seizes Chanda by the hair and cuts off his head, then Munda's, and carries both back to the goddess, laughing, as a gift. The goddess names her: because you've brought me Chanda and Munda, you'll be known as Chamunda.
So Kali comes not from outside but from the goddess's own brow, at the moment the threat comes close.
That's the Hindu teaching about Kali: she isn't a demon or a stranger.

teach.h: KALI MA: THE MOTHER'S FIERCE FACE.
teach.b: She is the Mother's own fierce face, the one that shows when her children are in danger. That's why so many families call her Kali Ma, mother, and keep her image at home.

teach.h: THE FIERCE FACE WAS INSIDE HER.
teach.b: One goddess, smiling and fierce at once.

how: Kali and Chamunda are worshiped in Hindu temples, and the seventh chapter of the Devi Mahatmya, where Kali springs from the goddess's brow and is named Chamunda, is recited as part of the whole text.

o: a battle cry that burns a general to ash
a Sanskrit text in praise of the goddess's glory
a prayer to Kali to keep demons from the house

games.q: the sixth and seventh chapters — tap the pairs.
p: burned to ash by one sound
springs from the goddess's frowning brow
named for killing Chanda and Munda

s: the goddess fights Dhumralochana for a long time
she makes one sound, hum, and he's burned to ash.
Kali is a demon the goddess has to tame
she springs from the goddess's own frowning forehead: the Mother's fierce face, not a stranger.
Kali brings the heads of Chanda and Munda back to the goddess
and the goddess names her Chamunda.

games.q: you're the goddess. Chanda and Munda come at you with a huge army, bows drawn. what happens?
o: you call the gods for help.
your face darkens, and Kali springs from your brow.
games.why: her face goes dark as ink with anger, and Kali springs from her forehead, destroys the army, and brings back Chanda's and Munda's heads.

practice: Bring to mind someone or something you'd stand up for, picture it threatened for just a moment, and notice what rises, a straighter back, a firm jaw, without acting on it: strength, not cruelty.

Then let calm come back alongside it, breath by breath, the way the goddess was smiling and fierce at once. If you pray, bow to Kali Ma, as so many families do, or to God in your own words; if not, let the breath hold both.

wordCard.voice: The Devi Mahatmya. Today, one syllable that burns a general to ash, and Kali, springing from the goddess's own brow, named Chamunda.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Cāmuṇḍā, the name the goddess gives Kali for killing Chanda and Munda.

carryVoice: Your line: Kali is the Mother's own fierce face. The same goddess smiled on the mountain. Week one of year four, done.

sources.ref: Devi Mahatmya, chapter 7 (Kali; Chanda and Munda; the name Chamunda)
